target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce school/work scheduling barriers for millions, especially low-income workers
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to give paid time off, so many low-income retail and service workers could still be scheduled to work and would not reliably get time to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would increase participation by removing scheduling barriers
objection: If low-income workers still have to work on Election Day, the main work-related barriers remain, so the holiday would leave those workers disadvantaged rather than broadly improving access.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would meaningfully boost turnout
objection: Research suggests that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that foreign precedent shows the holiday is feasible and workable
objection: State laws requiring employer time off to vote and automatic voter registration are more reliable ways to reduce voting barriers than relying on a holiday.

target: AG2’s objection that a federal holiday would still leave many low-income workers working and thus not help them
objection: School closures on federal holidays also remove childcare and school-day scheduling conflicts, which can be a major barrier for parents and caregivers, including low-income families.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would disadvantage low-income workers
objection: Low-income families often rely on predictable school schedules and have fewer childcare alternatives, so reducing school and childcare conflicts can actually improve their ability to vote even if some workplaces remain open.

target: AG2’s implication that only complete removal of every work barrier would count as a useful reform
objection: A holiday need not eliminate every barrier for every voter to be worthwhile; if it meaningfully reduces barriers for millions, that is enough to justify it.

target: AG2’s claim that private employers are not required to give paid time off on a federal holiday, so a holiday would not reduce work barriers
objection: Even without a legal paid-leave mandate, many employers reduce hours or close on federal holidays, so a holiday would often create real time away from work for at least some hourly workers.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reliably solve work-related voting barriers
objection: If a holiday reduces the number of people who must remain on shift during Election Day, it still reduces work-related voting barriers for millions of Americans, including many low-income hourly workers.

target: AG2’s argument that a holiday does not increase participation because it does not guarantee paid leave
objection: The proposal is about reducing voting time constraints and making voting easier to fit into people’s schedules; even partial reductions in those constraints can increase participation.

target: AG1’s claim that school-day timing and childcare conflicts make a holiday helpful
objection: The relevant question is whether the holiday reliably removes the barriers that matter most; school closures may help some parents, but they do not address the core work-schedule problem for low-income hourly workers.

target: AG1’s claim that school closures and a celebratory framing make the holiday broadly beneficial
objection: Because a federal holiday is not the same as a mandated paid day off, the policy’s effect depends on voluntary employer behavior rather than a legal guarantee, so it can preserve or worsen income-based access gaps.

target: AG1’s claim that school/childcare scheduling conflicts mean a holiday would improve access for low-income families
objection: If a policy does not reliably provide voting time to the least flexible workers, it risks leaving unequal voting access in place rather than fixing it.

target: AG1’s reliance on OECD countries that hold elections on weekends or holidays as evidence the idea works
objection: Other countries’ election-day holidays do not show that a U.S. federal holiday would work the same way, because U.S. private employers are not required to give paid time off under federal holiday law.

target: AG1’s claim that cross-party support and foreign precedent show the policy is workable
objection: The fact that many people support the idea does not answer whether it actually solves the problem; a popular policy can still be ineffective at increasing turnout.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reliably give low-income workers time to vote
objection: The proposal is aimed at reducing voting barriers broadly, not guaranteeing perfect paid leave for every worker; the absence of a perfect guarantee does not by itself show the holiday should be rejected.

target: AG2’s claim that foreign precedent does not help because U.S. holiday law differs
objection: OECD countries show that elections on weekends or holidays are compatible with functioning democracies, so the foreign precedent still supports the feasibility of the approach.

target: AG2’s claim that turnout research defeats the holiday proposal
objection: Even if the holiday is not the single most effective turnout reform, it can still be justified if it reduces scheduling barriers and elevates the civic meaning of voting.
